# Subsequence Matching and LCS under Cartesian-Tree Equivalence **Abstract** Two strings of the same length are said to _Cartesian-tree match_ (_CT-match_) if their Cartesian-trees are isomorphic [Park et al., TCS 2020]. Cartesian-tree matching is a natural model that allows for capturing similarities of numerical sequences. Oizumi et al. [CPM 2022] showed that subsequence pattern matching under CT-matching model (_CT-MSeq_) can be solved in _O(nm_loglog_n_) time, where **_n_** and **_m_** are text and pattern lengths, respectively. This current article follows this line of research, and gives the following new results: (1) An _O(nm_)-time CT-MSeq algorithm for binary alphabets.
(2) An _O_((_nm_)1-\(\epsilon\))-time conditional lower bound for the CT-MSeq problem on alphabets of size 4, for any constant \(\epsilon>0\), under the Orthogonal Vector Hypothesis (OVH).
Further, we introduce the new problem of _longest common subsequence under CT-matching_ (_CT-LCS_) for two given strings **_S_** and **_T_** of length **_n_**, and present the following results: Taketo Tsujimoto1, Yuki Yonemoto1∗, Hiroki Shibata2,

## 1 Introduction

### 1.1 Cartesian-tree equivalence of strings

In the recent large-scale data era, efficiently-computable string matching models which are capable of capturing _structural similarities_ are important for the analysis of numerical sequences such as time series. For instance, in financial markets, it seems more natural to focus on price fluctuation patterns in stock data, than to look for identical matches.

_Order-preserving matching_ (_OP-matching_) [1, 2] is a natural model for dealing with numerical sequences: Two strings _A_ and _B_ of length _n_ are said to be OP-match (or OP-equivalent) iff the lexicographical rank of _A_\[_i_\] in _A_ and that of _B_\[_i_\] in _B_ are equal for all \(1\le i\le n\).

_Cartesian-tree matching_ (_CT-matching_), first proposed by Park et al. [3], is another model for dealing with numerical sequences: Two strings _A_ and _B_ of length _n_ are said to be CT-match (or CT-equivalent) iff the (unlabeled) Cartesian-trees [4] of _A_ and _B_ are isomorphic. The CT-matching model is a relaxation of the OP-matching model, i.e., any OP-matching strings also CT-match, but the opposite is not true (for instance, \(A=\langle 1,1,2\rangle\) and \(B=\langle 1,1,1\rangle\) CT-match, but they do not OP-match). CT-matching has attracted attention in terms of pattern matching [3, 5], string periodicity [3], and indeterminate strings [6].

### 1.2 Subsequence matching under Cartesian-tree equivalence

In this article, we first deal with _subsequence_ matching under the CT-matching model (_CT-MSeq_): Given a text _T_ of length _n_ and a pattern _P_ of length _m_, find all minimal intervals \[_i,j_\] in _T_ such that _T_\[_i..j_\] contains a subsequence _Q_ that CT-matches _P_. This can be seen as the CT-matching version of the classical _episode matching_ [7]. Oizumi et al. [8] showed an algorithm that solves the CT-MSeq problem in _O(nm_loglog_n_) time and _O(n_log_m_) space for general ordered alphabets of arbitrary size. This is interesting since subsequence matching is NP-hard under OP-matching [9].

We revisit the CT-MSeq problem and present the following new results in the case of smaller alphabets:

(1) an _O(nm_)-time and _O(n_)-space CT-MSeq algorithm for binary alphabets.<tbc>

(2) an \(O((nm)^{1-\epsilon})\)-time conditional lower bound for the CT-MSeq problem on alphabets of size 4, for any constant \(\epsilon>0\), under the Orthogonal Vector Hypothesis (OVH).<tbc>

We achieve Result (1) with the _O(nm_)-time solution in the binary case by exploiting interesting properties of CT-matching on binary strings. Result (2), which extends the quadratic conditional lower bound for episode matching [10], implies that Oizumi et al.’s _O(nm_loglog_n_)-time solution for the CT-MSeq problem [8] is optimal up to logarithmic factors, unless OVH fails. We remark that OVH is implied by the famous Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH) [11].

## 1.3 LCS under Cartesian-tree model

We then extend our research to the well-studied class of string problem, _longest common subsequences_ (_LCSs_), that is one of the most fundamental models for measuring string similarities.

It is well known that, under the exact matching model, (the length of) an LCS of two given strings _S_ and _T_ of length _n_ can be computed in _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) time and space by standard dynamic programming, or in _O(n_<sup>2</sup>/log_n_) time and space [12] by the so- called "Four-Russians" method in the word RAM [13]. These quadratic and weakly subquadratic time bounds are believed to be essentially optimal, since a strongly subquadratic \(O(n^{2-\epsilon})\)-time solution to LCS with any constant \(\epsilon>0\) refutes OVH. Indeed, while there are a number of algorithms for computing LCS whose running times are dependent on other parameters (e.g. [14-17]), their worst-case time complexities remain \(\Omega(n^2)\).

As previously stated, subsequence matching under OP-matching is NP-hard. It is thus immediate that _order-preserving longest common subsequence_ (_OP-LCS_) is also NP-hard.

These arguments pose the following natural question - Is the _CT-LCS problem_ also polynomial-time solvable? Here, the CT-LCS problem is, given two strings _S_ and _T_ of length _n_, to compute (the length) of a longest string _Q_ such that both _S_ and _T_ have subsequences that CT-match _Q_. We answer this question affirmatively, by presenting the following efficient algorithms and conditional lowerbound:

(3) an _O(n_<sup>6</sup>)-time and _O(n_<sup>4</sup>)-space CT-LCS algorithm for general ordered alphabets.<tbc>

(4) an _O(n_<sup>2</sup>/log_n_)-time and space CT-LCS algorithm for binary alphabets.<tbc>

(5) an \(O(n^{2-\epsilon})\)-time conditional lower bound on the CT-LCS problem for alphabets of size 5, for any constant \(\epsilon>0\), under OVH.

While the _O(n_<sup>6</sup>)-time solution in the general case (Result (3)) is based on the idea of _pivoted Cartesian-trees_ from Oizumi et al. [8], our _O(n_<sup>2</sup>/log_n_)-time solution for the binary case (Result (4)) is built on a completely different approach that exploits interesting properties of CT-matching on binary strings, which we also use for the CT-MSeq problem.

## 1.4 Organization

The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 gives basic notions. In Section 3, we present combinatorial properties of CT-matching on binary strings, which will play central roles for our CT-MSeq and CT-LCS algorithms presented respectively in Sections 4.1 and 5.2. In Section 4, we present _O(nm_)-time solution for the CT- Mseq problem in the case of binary alphabets and our quadratic conditional lower<tbc>

In section 5, we present our _O(n_<sup>6</sup>)-time solution and _O(n_<sup>2</sup>)-time solution for the CT-LCS problem in the case of general ordered alphabets and binary alphabets, respectively, and quadratic conditional lower bounds for the CT-LCS problem. We conclude in Section 6.

## 2 Preliminaries

### 2.1 Basic notations: strings and vectors

For any positive integer _i_, we define a set \[_i_\]={1_,...,i_} of _i_ integers. Let \(\Sigma\) be an _ordered alphabet_ of size \(\sigma\). For simplicity, let \(\Sigma=\{0,\dots,\sigma-1\}\). An element of \(\Sigma\) is called a _character_. A sequence of characters is called a _string_. The _length_ of string _S_ is denoted by |_S_|. The empty string \(\varepsilon\) is the string of length 0. If _S=XYZ_, then _X_, _Y_ , and _Z_ are respectively called a _prefix_, _substring_, and _suffix_ of _S_. For a string _S_, _S_\[_i_\] denotes the _i_-th character of _S_ for each _i_ with \(1\le i\le|S|\). For each _i,j_ with \(1\le i\le j\le|S|\), _S_\[_i..j_\] denotes the substring of _S_ that begins at position _i_ and ends at position _j_. For convenience, let \(S[i..j]=\varepsilon\) for _i\>j_. We write \(\mathsf{min}(S)=\mathsf{min}\{S[i]|i\in[n]\}\) for the minimum character contained in the string _S_. For any \(0\le m\le n\), let \(\mathcal{I}_m^n\) be the set consisting of all _subscript sequence_ \(I=(i_1,\dots,i_m)\in[n]^m\) in ascending order satisfying \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_m\le n\). For subscript sequence \(I=(i_1,\dots,i_m)\in\mathcal{I}_m^n\), we denote by \(S_I=\langle S[i_1],\dots,S[i_m]\rangle\) the _subsequence_ of _S_ corresponding to _I_. For a subscript sequence _I_ and its elements \(i_s,i_t\in I\) with \(i_s\le i_t\), _I_\[_i<sub>s</sub>:i<sub>t</sub>_\] denotes the substring of _I_ that starts with _i<sub>s</sub>_ and ends with _i<sub>t</sub>_. For a sequence _T_<sub>1</sub>_,...,T<sub>k</sub>_ of strings, we define \(\prod_{i=1}^kT_i=T_1\cdots T_k\).

For a _d_-dimensional binary vector \(\alpha\in\{0,1\}^d\) and an integer \(1\le t\le d\), the _t_-th element in \(\alpha\) is denoted by \(\alpha[t]\). For two vectors \(\alpha,\beta\in\{0,1\}^d\), they are said to be _orthogonal_ if \(\sum_{i=1}^d\alpha[i]\beta[i]=0\) holds.

### 2.2 Subsequence matching and LCS under Cartesian-tree equivalence

For a string _S_, let min\_id(_S_) denote the least index _i_ such that _S_\[_i_\] is the smallest element in _S_.

**Definition 1** (Cartesian-tree) The _Cartesian-tree_ of a string _S_, denoted by CT(_S_), is the ordered binary tree recursively defined as follows: If \(S=\varepsilon\), then CT(_S_) is an empty tree, and otherwise, CT(_S_) is the tree rooted at _i_=min\_id(_S_) such that the left subtree of _i_ is CT(_S_\[1_..i_-1\]) and the right subtree of _i_ is CT(_S_\[_i_+1..|_S_|\]).

Fig. 1 shows CT(_S_) for a string \(S=\langle 5,8,2,6,4,7,4\rangle\) and CT(_S<sub>b</sub>_) for a binary string \(S_b=\langle 1,0,0,1,0,1,0\rangle\). As shown in Fig. 1, the Cartesian tree recursively splits the string based on the smallest character without considering the ordering of characters between the left and right subtrees, thereby expressing a flexible ordering structure of the characters.

For two strings _S_ and _T_ of equal length, the two Cartesian-trees CT(_S_) and CT(_T_) are _isomorphic_ if they have the same tree topology as ordered trees \[19\], which are tree data structures where the children of each node are ordered. We denote it by CT(_S_)=CT(_T_). We say that two strings _S_ and _TCT-match_ if CT(_S_)=CT(_T_).

**Definition 2** (CT-subsequence) A string _P_ is said to be a _CT-subsequence_ of a string _T_ if there is a subsequence _Q_ of _T_ such that CT(_Q_)=CT(_P_).

**Definition 3** (CT-occurrence interval) An interval \([\ell,r]\) in _T_ is said to be a _CT- occurrence interval_ for _P_ if there is a subsequence \(T[i_1]\cdots T[i_{|P|}]\) of \(T[\ell..r]\) such that \(\mathsf{CT}(T[i_1]\cdots T[i_{|P|}])=\mathsf{CT}(P)\), where \(\ell\le i_1\le\cdots\le i_{|P|}\le r\).

A CT-occurrence interval \([\ell,r]\) for _P_ in _T_ is said to be _minimal_ if no proper sub-interval of \([\ell,r]\) is a CT-occurrence interval for _P_ in _T_.

Our first problem is the following:

_Problem 1_ (CT-subsequence matching problem (CT-MSeq) \[8\]) Given two strings _T_ and _P_, find all minimal CT-occurrence intervals for _P_ in _T_.

Further, consider the Orthogonal Vector (OV) problem: Given two sets of _n<sub>A</sub>_ vectors _A_ and _n<sub>B</sub>_ vectors _B_ such that \(A,B\subset\{\alpha|\alpha\in\{0,1\}^d\}\), determine whether there exist two vectors \(\alpha,\beta\in A\) that are orthogonal. Regarding the OV problem, the following hypotheses are considered in the literature:

• **Orthogonal Vector Hypotheses (OVH):** For _n<sub>A</sub>=n<sub>B</sub>_, there are no \(\epsilon>0\) such that the OV problem can be solved in \(O(n_A^{2-\epsilon}\mathsf{poly}(d))\) time.<tbc>

• **Unbalanced Orthogonal Vector Hypotheses (UOVH):** Let \(0<\lambda\le 1\), there are no \(\epsilon>0\) such that the OV problem restricted to \(n_B=\Theta(n_A^\lambda)\) and \(d\le n^{o(1)}\) can be solved in \(O((n_An_B)^{1-\epsilon})\) time.

It is known that SETH implies OVH and UOVH \[11, 21\]. Thus, if OVH or UOVH is false, then SETH is also false.

## 3 Combinatorial properties of CT-matching on binary strings

In this section, we exploit new properties of CT-matching on binary strings, which we will use for designing efficient algorithms for CT-MSeq and CT-LCS on binary strings in Section 4.1 and Section 5.2, respectively.

We first recall the _parent-distance representation_ presented by Park et al. \[3\]: Given a string _S_\[1_..n_\], the parent-distance representation of _S_ is an integer string _PD(S_)\[1_..n_\], which is defined as follows:

\(PD(S)[i]=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
i-max_{1\le j<i}\{j|S[j]\le S[i]\} & \text{if such}j\text{exists}, \\
0 & \text{otherwise.}
\end{array}\right.\)

For example, the parent-distance representation of string \(S=\langle\mathtt{1},\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1},\mathtt{1},\mathtt{0},\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1}\rangle\) is \(PD(S)=\langle\mathtt{0},\mathtt{0},\mathtt{1},\mathtt{1},\mathtt{3},\mathtt{1},\mathtt{1}\rangle\).

**Lemma 1** (\[3\]) _Two strings S_<sub>1</sub> _and S_<sub>2</sub> _CT-match if and only if S_<sub>1</sub> _and S_<sub>2</sub> _have the same parent-distance representations._

Lemma 1 allows for determining whether two strings CT-match or not. We will only use this representation to guarantee the correctness of our algorithms for the binary case, and do not explicitly compute it.

## 4.1 Algorithm for binary CT-MSeq

Our algorithm for CT-MSeq on binary strings is based on Lemma 2 and Lemma 3. Firstly, we present some definitions to describe our algorithm. For any integers \(\ell\in[m]\) and \(j\in[n]\), let \(ND(\ell,j)\) be the largest integer _k_ such that _T_\[_k..j_\] contains a non- decreasing subsequence of length \(\ell\) and \(ND_0(\ell,j)\) be the largest integer _k_ such that _T_\[_k..j_\] contains a non-decreasing subsequence of length \(\ell\) _including at least one_ 0_’s._ Further, for a string _w_ and integers _i,j_ with \(i\in[|w|]\) and \(j\in[n]\), let _L<sub>w</sub>(i,j_) be the largest integer _k_ such that _T_\[_k..j_\] contains _w_\[1_..i_\] as a subsequence. If no such _k_ exists, let the values of \(ND(\ell,j)\), \(ND_0(\ell,j)\), and _L<sub>w</sub>(i,j_) be 0, respectively. For convenience, we define \(ND(\ell,0)=ND_0(\ell,0)=L_w(i,0)=0\) for any \(\ell,i\), and _w_. By the definition of _ND_, string \(T[ND(\ell,j)..j]\) is a minimal substring which contains a non-decreasing subsequence of length \(\ell\) if and only if \(ND(\ell,j-1)<ND(\ell,j)\) holds. Similarly, string \(T[ND_0(\ell,j)..j]\) is a minimal substring which contains a non-decreasing subsequence of length \(\ell\) including at least one 0’s if and only if \(ND_0(\ell,j-1)<ND_0(\ell,j)\) holds. Let \(q=min\{i\in[m]|P[i..m]\text{is a non-decreasing sequence}\}\). We also define M as the set of all minimal CT-occurrence intervals for _P_ over _T_. If _q_=1, i.e., _P_\[1_..m_\] is a non-decreasing sequence, by Observation 1, M is the set of all minimal intervals \([\ell,r]\) such that \(T[\ell..r]\) contains a non-decreasing subsequence of length _m_=|_P_|. ## _Computing ND_

Let \(prev_0(j)=\mathrm{max}(\{i<j|T[i]=0\}\cup\{0\})\). The values of _prev_<sub>0</sub>(_j_) for all \(j\in[n]\) can be computed in _O(n_) time by scanning _T_ from right to left. Let \(Z(\ell,j)\) be the staring position of the longest suffix of _T_\[1.._j_\] that contains \(0^\ell\) as a subsequence. If no such suffix exists, let \(Z(\ell,j)=0\). The values of _Z_ can be computed in _O(nm_) time by using the following recurrence:

\(Z(\ell,j)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
Z(\ell-1,prev_0(j)) & \text{if}T[j]=0, \\
Z(\ell,j-1) & \text{if}T[j]=1.
\end{array}\right.\)

Then, we show how to compute _ND_ (along with _Z_). We first initialize \(ND(\ell,0)=0\) for all \(\ell\in[m]\) and _ND_(1_,j_)=_j_ for all \(j\in[n]\). Then, we can compute _ND(m,j_) for incremental \(\ell=1,2,\dots,m\) and _j_=1,2_,...,n_ by using the following recurrence:

\(ND(\ell,j)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
\mathrm{max}\{Z(\ell,j),ND(\ell,j-1)\} & \text{if}T[j]=0, \\
ND(\ell-1,j-1) & \text{if}T[j]=1.
\end{array}\right.\)

We describe the above recurrence in detail in below. Let \(k=ND(\ell,j)>0\). By the definition of _ND_, there exists a subscript sequence \(I(k,j_1,\dots,j_{\ell-1})\) satisfying \(k<j_1<\cdots<j_{\ell-1}\le j\) such that _T_\[_k..j_\] contains a non-decreasing subsequence _T<sub>I</sub>_. If _T_\[_j_\]=0 and \(j_{\ell-1}=j\), then \(T[j_{\ell-1}]=0\) holds, and thus, \(T_I=0^\ell\). Hence, \(k=Z(\ell,j)\) holds. If _T_\[_j_\]=0 and \(j_{\ell-1}<j\), then _T_\[_k..j_-1\] also contains _T<sub>I</sub>_ as a subsequence. Thus, \(k=ND(\ell,j-1)\) holds. Finally, if _T_\[_j_\]=1, then \(j_{\ell-1}=j\) always holds, and thus, _T_\[_k..j_-1\] contains a non-decreasing subsequence of length \(\ell-1\). This leads to \(k=ND(\ell-1,j-1)\). Therefore, the above recurrence for _ND_ holds.

The time complexity of computing values of _ND_ is _O(nm_). Although _ND_ has \(\Theta(nm)\) values, the working space can be reduced to _O(n_) since we only refer to the \(\ell\)th or the \((\ell-1)\)th rows of _ND_ and _Z_ when computing the \(\ell\)th rows of _ND_ and _Z_, respectively.

**_Computing_** _ND_<sub>0</sub>

By the definitions of _ND_ and _ND_<sub>0</sub>, The following relation holds.

\(ND_0(\ell,j)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
ND(\ell,j) & \text{if}T[ND(\ell,j)]=0, \\
prev_0(ND(\ell,j)) & \text{otherwise.}
\end{array}\right.\)

This relation implies that, for every \(j\in[n]\), if we already have _ND(m_-|_w|,j_), then _ND_<sub>0</sub>(_m_-|_w|,j_) can be obtained _O_(1) time. Thus, we can compute the values of _ND_<sub>0</sub>(_m_-|_w|,j_) for all \(j\in[n]\) in _O(nm_) time using _O(n_) space.

**_Computing_** _L<sub>w</sub>_

We note that the definition of _L<sub>w</sub>_ is equivalent to the definition of the table, named _S_, used in \[7\] for the episode matching problem. Thus, we can use the same recurrence as in \[7\] to compute _L<sub>w</sub>_:

\(L_w(i,j)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
L_w(i-1,j-1) & \text{if}w[i]=T[j], \\
L_w(i,j-1) & \text{otherwise,}
\end{array}\right.\)

with the initialization _L<sub>w</sub>(i,_0)=0 for each \(i\in[|w|]\) and _L<sub>w</sub>_(0_,j_)=_j_+1 for each \(0\le j\le n\). We can obtain _L<sub>w</sub>_(|_w|,j_) for all \(j\in[n]\) in \(O(n|w|)\subseteq O(nm)\) time using _O(n_) space \[7\].

From the above discussion, we can compute the values of _ND(m,j_), _ND_<sub>0</sub>(_m_-|_w|,j_) and _L<sub>w</sub>_(|_w|,j_) for all \(j\in[n]\) in _O(nm_) time and _O(n_) space. Therefore, we obtain the following theorem:

**Theorem 1** _CT-MSeq on binary strings can be solved in O(nm_) _time and O(n_) _space._

Similarly to our algorithm for CT-MSeq for binary alphabets, which was proposed in Section 4.1, our algorithm for CT-MSeq on binary strings is based on Lemma 2 and Lemma 3.

Let _N_<sub>1</sub>(_S_) be the number of occurrences of 1 in string _S_, and _L_<sub>01</sub>(_S_) the length of the longest non-decreasing subsequence of _S_ that contains 0. ## 6 Conclusions and future work

This paper studied the two problems, CT-MSeq and CT-LCS, that relate to subsequences matching under the Cartesian-tree equivalence. We showed that quadratic and weakly subquadratic solutions exist for CT-MSeq and CT-LCS, respectively, in the case of binary alphabets. We also presented strongly subquadratic solutions are<tbc>

unlikely to exist for both CT-MSeq and CT-LCS for alphabets of sizes 4 and 5, respectively. In addition, we gave a polynomial time solution to CT-LCS in the case of general ordered alphabets.

A large gap remains between the _O(n_<sup>6</sup>)-time upper bound and the \(O(n^{2-\epsilon})\)-time lower bound for CT-LCS in the general case, and how to close this gap is an intriguing open question. Another open question is to close the gaps in the alphabet sizes for the subquadratic time complexities of CT-MSeq and CT-LCS.
